name: Mundum Neriyathum (Mundu and Neriyathu)
tagline: Kerala’s classic two‑piece cotton dress with the kasavu gold border
summary: Traditional two‑piece Kerala dress for women: a lower mundu and an upper neriyathu in cream cotton, often finished with a gold kasavu border and worn at Onam, Vishu and weddings.
description: Mundum Neriyathum (commonly called mundu and neriyathu or set mundu) is the traditional two‑piece dress worn by women in Kerala. The lower cloth (mundu) wraps at the waist and the upper cloth (neriyathu) drapes over the torso and shoulder, often over a blouse.

The festive version uses a kasavu — a gold or golden‑zari border — woven or stitched onto the cream/off‑white cotton. Kasavu pieces come from long handloom traditions centred in weaving clusters such as Kuthampully, Chendamangalam and Balaramapuram.

The set is emblematic of Kerala festivals and rituals: women wear it for Onam, Thiruvathira, Vishu, weddings and certain temple occasions. Contemporary variations include one‑piece Kerala saris inspired by the mundum neriyathum and ready‑to‑wear set mundus.
Today both handwoven kasavu and cheaper powerloom copies circulate in markets; many buyers look for handloom marks or GI‑tagged products when they want authentic weaving provenance.
highlights: Two unstitched pieces: lower mundu and upper neriyathu (set mundu)
Kasavu: gold/zari border used for festive and wedding versions
Worn for Onam, Vishu, Thiruvathira, weddings and folk dances (kaikottikali)
Handloom centres: Kuthampully, Chendamangalam, Balaramapuram weaving clusters
Modern one‑piece Kerala sarees and ready‑made sets built on the same tradition

sections.heading: Background
body: Mundum neriyathum traces to ancient Indian draped garments (antariya/uttariya). Over centuries it evolves into the two‑piece set associated with Kerala’s domestic and ritual life. The kasavu technique — a narrow gold/zari border — becomes a distinct regional style.

Weaving communities around Balaramapuram, Chendamangalam and Kuthampully supply traditional kasavu pieces; some products from these clusters carry geographical‑indication recognition to protect handloom identity.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend festival gatherings during Onam (late August–September) or Vishu (April) to see large numbers wearing set mundu and kasavu sarees; folk performances like kaikottikali and Thiruvathira feature the costume prominently.

Visit handloom cooperatives and cluster workshops (for example Kuthampully and Balaramapuram) to see weaving, ask about handloom vs powerloom kasavu, and buy authentic set mundu pieces or the one‑piece Kerala sari.

Learn basic draping: wrap the mundu at the waist like a skirt, tuck the neriyathu and pleat it across the torso or pin it on the shoulder. Ready‑to‑wear set mundus and stitched Kerala sarees make wearing easier for visitors.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Buy kasavu from recognised cooperatives or reputable shops; check weaving origin if you want handloom authenticity. Prices vary by weave, border width and whether real zari is used—confirm with the seller before purchase.

Care: wash gently in mild detergent, avoid harsh bleaching, and iron on moderate heat; for zari borders, prefer gentle handwash or professional care. For temple visits, follow local dress codes (generally modest dress with shoulders appropriately covered).

visitorInfo.bestTime: Festival seasons: Onam (Aug–Sep) and Vishu (April) to see the costume in its fullest public display.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Kerala’s major airports (Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram), railheads and interstate buses connect to weaving clusters and city markets—reach local hubs (Thrissur, Thiruvananthapuram, Kochi) then take local transport.
etiquette: Prefer handloom/cooperative shops for authentic kasavu and ask about the weave origin (Kuthampully, Chendamangalam, Balaramapuram).
If you want to wear set mundu for festivals, practise the drape beforehand or buy ready‑to‑wear sets for convenience.
Handle kasavu gently: avoid strong detergents and high heat; dry in shade to keep the gold border bright.
Respect local customs at temples and formal functions—cover shoulders and avoid casual or revealing styles.
